title: Sections [The section keyword]
description:
## What is a section?
So far you've used `section .data` and `section .text` without really knowing what they do.

A **section** tells the assembler and linker how to organize your program in memory. Each section has different permissions:

| Section | Contains | Read | Write | Execute |
|---------|----------|------|-------|---------|
| `.text` | Code | Yes | No | Yes |
| `.data` | Initialized variables | Yes | Yes | No |
| `.bss` | Uninitialized variables | Yes | Yes | No |
| `.rodata` | Constants | Yes | No | No |

When the OS loads your program, it puts each section in a different memory region with the right permissions. This is why:
- You can't write to `.text` (your code is read-only)
- You can't execute `.data` (your variables aren't code)
- You can't write to `.rodata` (constants are read-only)

If you violate these permissions, the OS kills your program with a **segfault**.

## Why separate sections?
1. **Security** - code can't be overwritten, data can't be executed
2. **Memory efficiency** - `.bss` takes zero space in the binary file
3. **Sharing** - `.text` and `.rodata` can be shared between multiple instances of the same program


---
## Question:
Why would writing to `.text` at runtime cause a segfault?
b1t: The CPU can't find the .text section
b3t: The OS marks .text as read-only and execute-only
b4t: You can write to .text, it just isn't recommended
